text: This is an orientation overview, not legal advice. SOX isn't a privacy law — it's a financial-reporting law. But the controls it demands are exactly what data governance builds. Plus three sector rules you'll hear named constantly: PCI DSS, GLBA, and FERPA.

Sarbanes-Oxley passed in 2002, after accounting scandals like Enron and WorldCom. It applies to publicly traded companies and their auditors. The goal: make sure financial reports are accurate, and that the controls behind them can actually be trusted.

Section 302 makes officers personally certify their financial reports are accurate. Section 404 requires management to assess internal controls, with independent auditor attestation. SOX also created the PCAOB, to oversee audits of public companies directly.

Section 404 in practice means: who can change financial data, is every change logged, are duties properly separated. That's access control, audit trails, and classification — the same infrastructure data governance builds for every other kind of sensitive data.

Three more names worth knowing: PCI DSS for payment card data, GLBA for financial-services customer information, FERPA for student education records. Each one governs a specific data category. Next lesson: Privacy by Design, and the seven principles behind GDPR's own Article 25.
